beats.trigger: Security
beats.got: Nothing new; this is the module title.

beats.trigger: It is important to involve the right stakeholders early, to follow best practices, and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: Three reading links, one of them for a different module, and I'm not sure which I was meant to do.

beats.trigger: **Evaluate** residual risk: what is left, and what future sessions need before touching the system
beats.got: The outcome is a reusable check plus a written statement of what risk remains. That is something I can show the CFO and legal.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I'm asked to think of my own checks before the agent proposes any. That's a good question.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: An agent's text becomes actions through tools, so a vague tool description or a misleading context can lead to a bad action. It's correct, but it's more mechanism than I needed.

beats.trigger: Leading companies are investing in enablement programmes, champions networks and training, and the ones that start early will be best placed.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output.
beats.got: Classical security assumes the software behaves the same way every time. That's the baseline for what comes next.

beats.trigger: The attack surface is the instruction set. The dangerous move is getting your agent to *decide* to do something harmful with access it has, through well-formed English in a document it reads.
beats.got: A document the agent reads can make it act, so even plain text in my pricing sources is part of the attack surface. I hadn't thought of it that way. The 'what may it read, change, send back to a human' questions are usable directly.

beats.trigger: Clear communication, strong sponsorship and regular follow-up remain the foundation
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: It is important to involve the right stakeholders early, to follow best practices, and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: nothing new; this is word for word the same as the first note.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: Context and access are separate dials: I've been turning context up, and the safety move is turning access down. Someone has to sign for where I set it.

beats.trigger: Expect it to cost you a feature.
beats.got: The cheapest mitigation is not connecting something, and that costs a feature. It overlaps with the previous slide, but the honest cost line is useful.

beats.trigger: Industry analysts expect agent adoption to accelerate significantly over the coming years.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: a skill is a reusable check you run again instead of re-prompting from memory.
beats.got: A skill is a check I can rerun, which is different from a clever prompt. That is the distinction I needed.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: Raw policy run against my own system. Some rules the files can check mechanically, and the rest need me or a person.

beats.trigger: Push back on anything that sounds like a generic GDPR brochure.
beats.got: I tell the agent what actually matters (pilot customer names, pricing data, the CFO's red lines) and it shapes the check around that. I can steer this.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: A long interview to build the skill with policy and agent-risk lenses. It's slow, but I can see where it ends.

beats.trigger: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: I can hand back the questions I can't answer and tell the agent to optimise for what I can't steer. That is a decisive move I'll reuse.

beats.trigger: The skill loads in your next session in this training directory.
beats.got: Install steps differ by runtime. It's housekeeping and I did it.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The skill is the output and the policy files are only source. It also says agent controls don't replace company ones. It's a recap and it repeats the earlier intro.

beats.trigger: agents are simply one more area where those principles apply.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: I confirm the skill I built is available in a fresh session.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit gave me three lists: compliant, violating, can't tell. Some things I thought were settled came back as 'can't tell', which is more honest than a green tick.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: A ranked risk report on my own agents. Seeing which one I'd have to accept and sign for is uncomfortable, and it's useful.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report. Walk in with that.
beats.got: When I can't resolve a risk I take the report, the quoted files, the mitigation and the residual to legal or security, and ask them one narrow question. That fits how our legal team wants to be approached.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: We handled one risk and a production agent needs all of them. It's blunt but fair, and it's short.

beats.trigger: Two things travel: the reusable check, and the root instructions file's rules for the risk you found.
beats.got: After the audit the agent writes up to five rules into the root instructions file, so the next session starts with what I learned. This still helps on Monday without me rebuilding it.

beats.trigger: To share, give a teammate the skill and install it in their runtime.
beats.got: A skill is a method a teammate can install, so it's one way my fourteen people could share work. It doesn't settle ownership, and Module 7 covers that.

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework: one sentence per case about the missing check. The 'Your call' reads like a mild threat.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Read two cases, Mata v. Avianca and Deloitte Australia, and ask what check was missing. Those are cases I would use with my CFO.

take_homes: Give the agent less access, not just more context. The safest option is often not opening the door, and that costs a feature I have to name and sign for.
A skill is a reusable check, not a clever prompt. Mine runs a policy lens and an agent-risk lens, and it gives me compliant, violating and 'can't tell'.
When the check can't resolve a risk, I take the narrow question and the evidence to legal or security, along with the mitigation and the residual.

monday.move: Run the packaged agent-audit on the pilot-cohort brief agent for the usage-pricing work, and write down the residual risk for the pricing working group.
monday.who: Me first, then one person from legal or IT on the 'can't tell' rows.
monday.when: Monday morning, before I send the brief.
monday.stop_condition: Stop when the policy report and the risk report exist and the residual is named, even if it isn't solved.
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for context files and skills, so the check lives on my machine until we sort that.

misconception.why: I came in thinking better prompts were the skill. The module showed that the reusable check, the access scoping and the written residual matter more than the prompt wording. I haven't dropped the belief entirely, because the interview prompts still mattered.

one_line: Good hour on what to take away from an agent and how to rerun the check, but cut the repeated 'context' filler slides and the same paragraph appearing three times.
